253.title: You haven't been there (Avot 2:4)
253.hook: Hillel: don't separate from the community; don't judge until you've stood in their place
253.howItsDone: Hillel's warning is studied alongside the teaching to judge every person favorably, as a daily habit of thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel's mirror: do God's will as your own. Your line was want what's good. Did you find a reason to want it? Today, Hillel is back. Day two hundred fifty-three.

The woman in the checkout line snaps at her kid, and everyone around her silently decides what kind of mother she is. The coworker who's been late three times this month. The neighbor who never mows his lawn. These verdicts arrive in an instant, and they feel very sure. What we don't see is the hospital visit that morning, or the second job, or the thing nobody talks about at home. Hillel, the gentle sage from the roof in the snow, has five short warnings in chapter two. The middle one is about exactly this.
screen: `THE MOTHER IN THE CHECKOUT LINE.` → `AN INSTANT, VERY SURE.` → `WHAT WE DON'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Here are Hillel's warnings. Don't separate yourself from the community. Don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Don't say something that can't be understood, hoping it'll be understood later. And don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you won't. Look at the middle one. Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Makom in Hebrew: his place, his spot, where he's standing. Not until you've heard about it. Until you've gotten there. Now look at the line right before it: don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. The Talmud tells of a high priest who served faithfully for eighty years, and then, at the very end, left the path of the sages. Nobody is beyond slipping. Put those two lines side by side and you see what Hillel is doing. You can't be too sure about yourself, and you can't be too sure about the other person. You don't know how you'd act in their place, because you've never stood there. Some teachers point out something quietly radical in the wording. Can you ever really reach another person's place? Their childhood, their body, their worst morning? Maybe never completely. Which would mean the judgment always waits. That doesn't mean anything goes. Jewish law has courts and judges. But in everyday life, Hillel asks for a pause, and a little humility, before the verdict.
screen: `HILLEL'S FIVE WARNINGS.` · `UNTIL YOU'VE REACHED HIS PLACE.` · `DON'T BE SURE OF YOURSELF.` · `CAN YOU EVER REACH IT?` · then, large: `YOU HAVEN'T BEEN THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand in someone's place. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you've judged lately. Don't argue about whether you were right. Just imagine waking up in their bed this morning. Their worries. Their body. Their bank account. The conversation they're dreading. Walk through their morning slowly, until they get to the moment you judged. Notice if anything shifts. The bell holds the time.
You haven't been there. Hillel's warning: don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place, and don't be too sure of yourself either.
Your line: you haven't been there. Today, when a quick judgment rises, hold it back once, and wonder what their morning was like. Day two hundred fifty-three.

254.title: Be a mensch (Avot 2:5)
254.hook: Hillel: where there are no decent people, strive to be one
254.howItsDone: Calling someone a mensch is a common Jewish compliment for integrity and kindness, and parents and teachers often quote Hillel's line when urging children to do the decent thing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel said don't judge anyone until you've reached their place. Your line was you haven't been there. Did you hold back a judgment? Day two hundred fifty-four.

A man drops a bag of groceries on a busy sidewalk. Oranges rolling everywhere. Twenty people see it. Everyone slows down, looks, and keeps walking, because surely somebody else will help. Then one person stops, crouches down, and starts picking up oranges. And suddenly two more people stop too. You probably have a word for the first person. If you've spent any time around Jewish grandparents, the word is mensch. Today we find where it comes from, in one line of Hillel.
screen: `ORANGES ON THE SIDEWALK.` → `TWENTY PEOPLE KEEP WALKING.` → `ONE PERSON STOPS.`

segments.voice: Mensch is Yiddish, from the German word for a human being. But in Yiddish it grew into something more: a person of integrity, someone decent and kind and trustworthy, someone who does the right thing without being asked. Calling someone a real mensch is one of the highest compliments there is, and it has nothing to do with money, fame or cleverness. The idea behind it is old. In Pirkei Avot, Hillel gives a short list of who can and can't do what. A person who's too bashful can't learn, because they won't ask questions. A person who's short-tempered can't teach. And then his final line: in a place where there are no people, try to be a person. The Hebrew for person there is ish, and it clearly means more than just being human. It means someone who stands up. When nobody is stepping forward, you step forward. When nobody is being decent, you be the decent one. Commentators read it a couple of ways. The plain way: when no one else is taking responsibility, take it. Another way: even where there's no one around to see you, still act like a real person. Either way, Hillel's word is strive. Try hard. It isn't easy to be the first one to stop on the sidewalk. Everyone else keeping on walking pulls on you. Being a mensch means feeling that pull and crouching down anyway. And notice what happens once one person does: others often follow.
screen: `MENSCH: A DECENT HUMAN BEING.` · `TOO BASHFUL TO LEARN.` · `WHERE NO ONE IS, BE SOMEONE.` · `STRIVE: IT ISN'T EASY.` · then, large: `BE A MENSCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the room that needs a mensch. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place you'll be today, a meeting, a family chat, a train, a classroom, where something usually goes undone because everyone waits for someone else. The dishes after dinner. The new person nobody talks to. The joke that goes too far. Picture yourself being the one who moves first. Just once. Feel what that's like. The bell holds the time.
Mensch. Yiddish for a human being, and for a decent one. Hillel said: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person.
Your line: be a mensch. Today, when everyone's waiting for someone else to do the decent thing, be the first one to do it. Day two hundred fifty-four.

255.title: The skull on the water (Avot 2:6)
255.hook: Hillel sees a skull floating and says: because you drowned others, you were drowned
255.howItsDone: Jewish teaching speaks of 'measure for measure' (middah keneged middah) as a pattern in how the world works, while leaving judgment to God and the courts rather than to private revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, oranges on the sidewalk and Hillel's line: where there are no people, strive to be a person. Your line was be a mensch. Were you the first to move? Day two hundred fifty-five.

Pirkei Avot is mostly sayings. Short, wise, a little abstract. And then, right in the middle of chapter two, there's a scene out of a ghost story. Hillel is at the water's edge. Something is floating on the surface, turning slowly in the current. He looks closer. It's a human skull. Hillel doesn't scream, and he doesn't walk away. He speaks to it. And what he says is only a handful of words, in Aramaic, the everyday language of his time.
screen: `A SCENE, NOT A SAYING.` → `SOMETHING ON THE WATER.` → `HILLEL SPEAKS TO IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what Hillel says to the skull. Because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, the ones who drowned you will be drowned. That's the whole thing. The Mishnah doesn't say whose skull it was, or where, or when. It doesn't tell us how Hillel knew. We're only given the words. The first half sounds like simple payback: you did it, so it was done to you. The rabbis have a name for this idea, measure for measure. What a person sends out tends to come back in kind. But look at the second half, because that's where the saying turns. The ones who drowned you will be drowned too. The people who killed this man aren't heroes of justice. They've just joined the cycle. And the cycle doesn't stop with them. Violence answered by violence doesn't end anything. It just hands the drowning on to the next person. Commentators are careful here, and so should we be. This isn't a claim that everyone who suffers must have deserved it. Hillel is speaking to one skull, not about every victim in the world. Some commentators read it as a statement about God's justice, which works in ways people can't see and don't get to take into their own hands. So the saying ends up as a warning in two directions. Don't be the one who drowns others. And don't appoint yourself to drown the drowner. Harm comes back. The only way out of the circle is for someone to stop pushing.
screen: `A SKULL, AND A FEW WORDS.` · `MEASURE FOR MEASURE.` · `THE DROWNERS WILL BE DROWNED.` · `SOMEONE HAS TO STOP PUSHING.` · then, large: `HARM COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small circle of harm. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life where hurt is going back and forth. A sibling who snipes and you snipe back. A coworker you both undercut. A comment section. Nothing dramatic. Just a small circle. Now imagine the next turn is yours, and you simply don't take it. No reply in kind. Picture the circle slowing down. The bell holds the time.
The skull on the water. Hillel's words to it: because you drowned others, they drowned you, and those who drowned you will be drowned.
screen: `THE SKULL ON THE WATER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: harm comes back. Today, when someone hands you a small hurt, don't hand it back. Let the circle stop with you. Day two hundred fifty-five.

256.title: More isn't more (Avot 2:7)
256.hook: more flesh, more worms; more possessions, more worry; more Torah, more life
256.howItsDone: Giving tzedakah, charity understood as justice, is a central Jewish practice, and some households keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel spoke to a skull on the water, and warned about the circle of revenge. Your line was harm comes back. Did you let a small hurt stop with you? Day two hundred fifty-six.

The shoes, the gadget, the bigger apartment: the thing someone really wanted, finally bought. For a few days, it was wonderful. And then, quietly, it came with things. A password to remember. A warranty to register. A thing to insure, to clean, to worry about being scratched. A rented storage unit is a monument to this feeling. Hillel noticed it too, and turned it into a saying with a beat. It sounds almost like a chant.
screen: `THE THING YOU REALLY WANTED.` → `IT CAME WITH THINGS.` → `A SAYING LIKE A CHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's how Hillel's list begins. More flesh, more worms. More possessions, more worry. It's blunt. A body fattened on luxury ends in the same grave as everyone else's. And the more you own, the more you have to guard. In Hebrew it has a beat: marbeh nekhasim, marbeh de'agah. More things, more worry. The list goes on through the households of his ancient world, with a few lines about servants and wives that read uncomfortably today, and are honestly part of the text. And then the list turns. More Torah, more life. More sitting in study, more wisdom. More counsel, more understanding. More tzedakah, more giving to those in need, more peace. See what Hillel's doing. He isn't against more. He's saying some kinds of more shrink you, and some kinds of more grow you. Possessions pile up and need guarding. Wisdom, understanding and generosity pile up and set you free. And the list ends with a surprise about generosity. Giving looks like it should leave a person with less. Hillel says it leaves you with more peace. Then he adds one more line: a person who has gained a good name has gained it for himself, but a person who has gained words of Torah has gained life in the world to come. A good name is precious, he seems to say, but it stays here. What you learn and give goes further. So the carry is short: more isn't more. The question is always: more of what?
screen: `MORE FLESH, MORE WORMS.` · `MORE THINGS, MORE WORRY.` · `THE LIST TURNS: MORE TORAH, MORE LIFE.` · `MORE GIVING, MORE PEACE.` · then, large: `MORE ISN'T MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to let go of. Settle, and breathe. Picture walking slowly through your home. A closet. A drawer. A shelf. Look for one thing you're keeping that you don't need, and that someone else could use. A coat. A book. A pan. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it. Then picture it in someone else's hands, being useful. See if the tug loosens. The bell holds the time.
More isn't more. Hillel's list: more things, more worry; but more learning, more life, and more giving, more peace.
Your line: more isn't more. Today, give one thing away, and notice whether you end up with more worry or more peace. Day two hundred fifty-six.

257.title: A good heart (Avot 2:9)
257.hook: Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students the best path; the answer that wins is a good heart
257.tomorrow: repent a day before you die
257.howItsDone: This mishnah is studied as a portrait of character, and 'lev tov' is still an everyday Hebrew phrase for a kind, good-hearted person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's chant: more things, more worry, more giving, more peace. Your line was more isn't more. Did you give something away? Day two hundred fifty-seven.

A teacher gives his five students one assignment. No test, no essay. Just: go out and look at the world, and come back and tell me the one good path a person should hold on to. Five students. Five answers. And then the teacher picks one, and explains why it wins. The teacher is Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the student of Hillel, remembered as the sage who kept Jewish learning alive when Jerusalem fell to Rome. And the winning answer is two Hebrew words: lev tov.
screen: `FIVE STUDENTS, ONE ASSIGNMENT.` → `YOCHANAN BEN ZAKKAI.` → `TWO WORDS WIN.`

segments.voice: Yochanan ben Zakkai says to his students: go out and see which is the good way a person should cling to. The five come back. Rabbi Eliezer says: a good eye, meaning a generous way of looking at people. Rabbi Joshua says: a good friend. Rabbi Yose says: a good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: someone who sees what's coming, who thinks about the results of what they do. And Rabbi Elazar ben Arach says: a good heart. Then the teacher speaks. I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arach, because his words include all of yours. Think about why. A good eye, generous seeing, starts in the heart. A good friend and a good neighbor are what a good heart becomes when it lives near people. Even seeing what's coming depends on caring about who gets hurt. The heart is the root, and the others are branches. In the Bible's Hebrew, the heart isn't just feelings. It's where a person thinks, decides and wants. So lev tov isn't only warmth. It's a whole inner life pointed toward the good. And then the Mishnah runs the same exercise backward. Yochanan asks: which is the bad way a person should stay away from? A bad eye, a bad friend, a bad neighbor, someone who borrows and doesn't pay back, and, from Elazar ben Arach again, a bad heart. And again the teacher says: his words include all of yours. Five answers, one root. Everything else grows from the heart.
screen: `GO OUT AND SEE THE GOOD WAY.` · `EYE, FRIEND, NEIGHBOR, FORESIGHT.` · `HIS WORDS INCLUDE ALL OF YOURS.` · `THE HEART IS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `LEV TOV: A GOOD HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tend the root. Settle, and breathe. Put a hand on your chest if that feels natural. Notice the heart going on quietly without you asking it to. Now think of the four branches. A good eye: someone you could see more generously. A good friend: someone you could reach out to. A good neighbor: someone near you who needs something. Foresight: one choice today whose results you could think through. Let each one come back to the heart. The bell holds the time.
Lev tov. A good heart: the answer Yochanan ben Zakkai chose, because it holds all the others inside it.
Your line: a good heart. Today, before one decision, ask what a good heart would choose, and let the rest follow from that. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

screen: `DAY 257 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: REPENT A DAY BEFORE YOU DIE.`

258.title: Repent a day before you die (Avot 2:10)
258.word: Repent a day before you die
258.hook: Rabbi Eliezer: repent one day before your death, and no one knows the day, so every day
258.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats teshuvah, returning, as possible every day, not only on Yom Kippur, and the traditional bedtime prayers include a moment of forgiving others before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five students, five answers, and the one that held all the others. Your line was a good heart. What did a good heart choose? Today, one of those students speaks. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Rabbi Eliezer's students heard him say something that sounded impossible: repent one day before your death. So they asked the obvious question. How is anyone supposed to know which day that is? Eliezer was one of the five students from yesterday, the one his own teacher compared to a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. He had heard a great deal and lost none of it. And his answer takes a far-off day and sets it down right here, in this one.
screen: `AN IMPOSSIBLE INSTRUCTION.` → `WHICH DAY IS THAT?` → `A CISTERN THAT LOSES NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Eliezer said three things. Let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own. Don't be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. That last one is the riddle, and the Talmud records his answer to the students who asked about it. Does anyone know the day he'll die? All the more reason to repent today, in case you die tomorrow. Then all your days will be spent in repentance. The word is teshuvah. It's usually translated repentance, but it really means return, or turning. You notice you've wandered off the path, and you turn back toward it. No groveling required, no drama. Just a turn. The Talmud then tells a parable. A king invited his servants to a banquet, but didn't say when. The wise ones dressed in their best and waited by the palace door. After all, a palace is never short of anything; the feast could start any minute. The foolish ones went off to their work, saying, there's no banquet without a lot of preparation first. Suddenly the king called them in. The wise walked in dressed and ready. The foolish came in dirty from work, and weren't allowed to sit at the table. The verse that goes with it is in Ecclesiastes, which in the JPS translation reads, "Let thy garments be always white." Not out of fear. Just ready. Rabbi Eliezer's advice isn't a threat. It's a schedule. If today might be the day, then today is the day to turn.
screen: `THREE PIECES OF ADVICE.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE DAY.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `THE KING'S BANQUET.` · then, large: `LET THY GARMENTS BE ALWAYS WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small turn, today. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the day so far, slowly, from waking up until now. Notice one moment where you drifted from the person you mean to be. A sharp word. A shortcut. A kindness skipped. Don't argue with it, and don't punish yourself. Just name it. Then picture the turn back: what would one small step in the right direction look like, before tonight? If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Repent a day before you die. Rabbi Eliezer's riddle: nobody knows the day, so turn back today, and every day is a day of teshuvah.
screen: `REPENT A DAY BEFORE YOU DIE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: repent today. Find one turn you've been saving for someday, a sorry, a habit, a call, and make the first small move before you sleep. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

259.title: A good eye (Avot 2:11)
259.hook: an evil eye, the bad urge and hatred of people drive a person out of the world
259.howItsDone: In Jewish ethics, ayin tovah, a good eye, means generosity and gladness at others' good fortune, and it is often taught alongside the laws of giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Eliezer said repent one day before you die, and nobody knows the day. Your line was repent today. Did you take one thing off the someday list? Day two hundred fifty-nine.

A friend posts a photo of her new house. You tap the heart. And somewhere under the heart, there's a small, sour feeling. Why her? She didn't even work that hard. You'd never say it out loud. But you felt it. Everybody has. Two days ago, Rabbi Eliezer's answer to the teacher's question was a good eye. Today, another of those five students, Rabbi Joshua, describes the opposite. And he says it doesn't just spoil your mood. It drives you out of the world.
screen: `THE HEART UNDER THE PHOTO.` → `A SMALL, SOUR FEELING.` → `RABBI JOSHUA'S WARNING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Joshua says three things drive a person out of the world: an evil eye, the bad urge, and hatred of people. Start with the evil eye, because it's not what you might think. In the Mishnah, an evil eye isn't a curse or a spell. It's a way of looking. A stingy, begrudging eye. The eye that sees someone else's good fortune and wishes, a little, that they didn't have it. A good eye is the opposite: an eye that's glad when others do well, and that gives freely. The Bible has a phrase for this. Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye is blessed, because he shares his bread with the poor. The Hebrew there is tov ayin, literally good of eye. Then the bad urge, the yetzer hara, the pull toward the selfish thing. And hatred of people, of anyone at all. Now, why would these drive you out of the world? Commentators give several answers. One is simple: they make you miserable, and wear your life down. Another is that they cut you off. If every friend's good news stings, you slowly stop being able to be with people. You end up alone in a crowd. The good eye opens the world back up. When you can be glad for others, their joy becomes a little bit yours. And that closes a week of Hillel and his heirs: you haven't been there, be a mensch, harm comes back, more isn't more, a good heart, repent today, and now, a good eye.
screen: `THREE THINGS DRIVE YOU OUT.` · `THE EVIL EYE: A BEGRUDGING LOOK.` · `TOV AYIN: GOOD OF EYE.` · `ALONE IN A CROWD, OR GLAD.` · then, large: `A GOOD EYE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish one person well, for real. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose good news stung a little. A promotion, a trip, a new relationship. Don't pretend the sting isn't there. Just notice it. Then, slowly, picture them enjoying what they have. Their face. Their relief. Let yourself wish it for them, sincerely, with no but at the end.
